I welcome the opportunity to engage you in a civil discussion about this.

While it goes without saying that no one of us speaks for all of us, feeling as though I belong has convinced me that I'm not alone in my opinions. Nevertheless, I will state that these are indeed my opinions, regardless however informed by observation I feel them to be. That said, my perception of how things work here is as follows:

What Are Downvoats, Really?

It is no longer a question as to whether downvoats are a signal of disapproval. They absolutely are, and a strong one at that.
The question has become, "Is that a bad thing?" and I believe it is not.

I look at this site as though it were an emergent mind wherein every single user is a neuron. If we only ever hear where people agree, though, we are missing easily half of the communication. An idea that has 30 upvoats in such a setting also has the fidelity of magnitude, to tell us how important it is--how many users' lives it influenced, how many people it touched, how relevant it is:

30 upvoats, 0 downvoats = This is irrelevant. Only 30 people even noticed.
330 upvoats, 300 downvoats = This is pretty serious! 630 people care about this one way or another, and the split decision means there's a lot of turmoil in it!
2418 upvoats, 2388 downvoats = This is a huge deal affecting many lives and it's such a close call that the details really deserve a thorough perusal.

This is impossible if only upvoats exist. If only upvoats existed, we'd only get half of the picture. And the larger an item would be, the more overwhelmingly positive people would just assume it is, except for those in the comments striving to present their counter evidence and being completely overlooked by the majority. Here we would have a system that:

  1. Encourages verbal abuse as the only means of dissent and creates more work for the moderation body who would have to crack down, Waste, Waste, Waste!
  2. Lobotomizes the context and only produces a saccharine, one-note presentation of content, akin to serving prescriptions without warning labels..
  3. Is ripe for the abuse of sock puppet voat bots to come in and brigade something to synthetic popularity. If the content isn't against the rules, not even reporting could remove it.

In short, Downvoats are the brakes of this car. They are the sanity check. They are our capacity for Skepticism. They are the "Wait WHAT? Seriously?" of this community.

What Do Downvoats Mean?

There will always be a persistent idea that Downvoats aren't supposed to be a "disapproval" or "disagreement" button. However, even though that's what downvoats are to individual users, the net emergent effect is closer to what Downvoats are supposed to be: A guide.

When a user sees content they find objectionable in the community to which they subscribe, it is their duty to do right by their community by downvoating. They could be feeling any range of very unfriendly emotions... but when they click that button, regardless of what prompted it, the impulse is sanitized to a simple, standardized format, a poke of dissent. No matter how angry, frustrated, or disgusted the userbase may be, at the end of the day, the offending post is told only ONE THING: "This is not the correct way to satisfy the values of this subverse. Please try again."

You see, to the users, Downvoats are a tool. To a submitter of content, though, the downvoats are an inherent part of their environment; an environment their submission must be able to survive--and its survival ability is based upon how well it, as above, satisfies the values of the subverse. downvoats are the only way to communicate that. It is a slog through brute force trial-and-error. Some subverses are kind enough to put some guidelines in the sidebar, but there will always be some need to grow and adapt, and this will ever provide better content in the long run. It's a messy process, to be sure, and sometimes very inconvenient. But without them, no such communication would be happening at all.

Of What Measure is a Barrier?

When starting out at first, it's admittedly daunting. A treacherous trek with little guidance through territory that seems hostile.

But the source of much of this trepidation is actually a means of perception.

No one will ever be wounded, crippled, or detained by downvoats. If a bad submission is made, it's frustrating, but it does not disable a user's account, nor does it function as a ban. Nothing prevents them from submitting again except perhaps their own fear. If they learned from their previous attempt, if they are trying something new, if they have caught rarest ghostly glimpse of some way they can do it better, they are welcome to.

The only ones who do not overcome this hurdle are the ones who stop trying. The only real limit is the self. So, are downvoats a barrier? Only if you allow them to be. Again, most subverses go so far as to frame exactly what the spirit of their pursuit is in the sidebar, but no amount of text is ever going to be an effective replacement for experience.

You're close. In the end, it is actually a blend:
Having upvoats and downvoats is a vital component in the nervous system of the community as a whole.
The survival of the whole lives within the individual's commitment to being part of that system by utilizing those components.

We are the neurons, and upvoats as well as downvoats are the synapses that allow us to talk to one another in an accessible, quickly understood way (taking less time than reading a comment). In the act of this short form conversation, idea-like patterns form. Voat thinks like a single mind only because all its 'cells' can carry (and effectively communicate) their differences. I believe I've heard much the same about the human brain; that it's a messy tangle of conflict until it averages out, and the average becomes our consciousness.

Your real life example is an excellent one. Lack of "negative votes", I believe, is one of the biggest things that holds back our 'first past the post' electoral system. Indeed, many people only vote for one person in particular specifically to prevent one other person from winning. If they could just negative vote for the one person they don't want, it would free up those who actually one one person in particular to win and potentially pry us out of our two-party rut.

It is my fear that losing this voice that downvoats give us will result in a system like that. One that is blind to the controversy, deaf to the other side of the story, enfeebled in the face of uncomfortable truths. This is why I brought up facebook in my first response to you.

Facebook is a wasteland of clickbait, baby pictures, dumb memetic image macros, and insipid one-sided whining. Stupid things soar to the top not because they're right, but purely because they're blandly entertaining, and no matter HOW large a population may find it to be disingenuous, or ignorant, or cruel, or disrespectful, or even just plain irrelevant, they no longer have a voice. Just because 4,000 people liked it, it's going viral, never mind the 40,000 who disagree.

And I suppose that's one more way I never thought of to pose this:
I believe that disagreement has as much right to be heard as agreement.
I believe it hurts us to plug our ears to disagreement in the same way that humans who are neurologically incapable of feeling pain constantly lead short, horrifically brutal lives, walking on broken limbs, picking at open wounds, greeting their own blood with curiosity rather than caution, and carrying infections of all kinds back for the rest of us to become afflicted with.

So what should we call this social injury? A demise of critical thinking? Some other, more bluntly insulting term?
I can't say for sure, but it certainly is one.
